title: Like Confessing a Murder: Darwin's Private Theory
subtitle: Darwin's transmutation notebooks, his trusted readers, and the Vestiges storm, London and Down, 1837–1845
intro: In July 1837, less than a year after the Beagle docked, Charles Darwin opened a small notebook and began to think about the 'transmutation of species'. Within fifteen months he had the mechanism, scrawled in Notebook D on 28 September 1838 after reading Malthus. He did not publish it for twenty years. This chapter covers the first seven of them, from the notebooks to the essay of 1844 and the storm over Vestiges in 1845, when the idea lived on paper in one study and in a handful of letters.

The record is mostly private notebooks, a terse pocket journal, two marriage memoranda and dated letters, not diaries. The notebooks were printed only in the twentieth century; Darwin cut pages from them for later use. Laid beside them are the letters of the very few people he told: Emma Wedgwood, who heard of his religious doubts before their marriage; Joseph Hooker, a young botanist he barely knew, who received the confession 'like confessing a murder' in January 1844; and Leonard Jenyns, a clergyman friend told the same autumn.

Around this inner circle stand people who were named but not told. In July 1844 Darwin ranked possible editors for his essay should he die: Lyell first, Henslow with question marks, Hooker added in the margin. No letter of this period shows Lyell or Henslow responding to the theory, and Jenyns's reply is lost; those gaps are marked on their eyes. Darwin's father, who advised him to hide his doubts, is known only from his son's memory forty years later.

In October 1844 an anonymous book, Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, said in public much of what Darwin believed in private. Its author, the Edinburgh publisher Robert Chambers, was hiding a name as carefully as Darwin was hiding a theory, with letters routed through Alexander Ireland in Manchester. Darwin and Hooker read it in parallel; Adam Sedgwick, Darwin's old geology teacher, answered it with fury; Tennyson sent for it eagerly; and a young collector in Wales, Alfred Russel Wallace, decided it was a hypothesis worth testing.

Read together, the records show what secrecy protected and what it cost. It gave Darwin time to accumulate facts and rehearse objections, and the Vestiges uproar showed him exactly which arguments he would face. It also left the theory dependent on one fair copy, one letter to his wife and a few correspondents, and it set up the scramble of 1858, told in Volume IV.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Many of Darwin's letters carry only a weekday or no year, so dates in square brackets are supplied by the editors of the Darwin Correspondence Project from postmarks and content. The pocket Journal was begun in 1838 and its entries for 1837 were written in afterwards. The Autobiography was written in 1876, printed in cut form in 1887 and in full in 1958, so its dates are later recollections.
seam: For seven years one man kept a theory in notebooks and tested it on a few trusted readers by letter, one at a time, each confession smaller than the truth. Meanwhile another man published a similar idea with his own name hidden, and the public reaction showed the cost of speaking too soon. The records show secrecy giving time and armour, but also leaving the idea in a single copy and a letter to a wife. Like the private world of Dark Matter, the hidden version was real long before anyone else could see it.

eyes.name: Charles Robert Darwin
eyes.role: Naturalist, aged 28 in July 1837, a year back from the Beagle voyage; secretary of the Geological Society 1838–41; married from January 1839; at Down House, Kent, from September 1842
eyes.side: English gentleman naturalist; Unitarian-Anglican Wedgwood–Darwin family
eyes.where: London (Great Marlborough Street, then Upper Gower Street), Maer and Shrewsbury on family visits, Down House from 1842

waypoints.label: Maer Hall: engagement Nov 1838, wedding Jan 1839
Shrewsbury and Maer: pencil sketch, June 1842

eyes.form: private notebooks, pocket journal, private memoranda and dated letters; an autobiography written later (1876)
eyes.authenticity: Notebooks B–E and M–N survive at Cambridge University Library (DAR 121–126), many pages cut out by Darwin himself and later recovered; printed only in the 20th century (de Beer 1960–67; Barrett 1974; Barrett et al. 1987). His pocket 'Journal' (DAR 158) was begun in 1838 with earlier years written in retrospectively. Letters are edited by the Darwin Correspondence Project, whose bracketed dates are editorial. The Autobiography (1876) was first printed, cut, in 1887; the full text only in 1958.
eyes.bio: Within months of landing from the Beagle he privately concluded that species change, and spent seven years writing the idea out only for himself. His notebooks swing between species, breeding, mind and materialism, while his letters show him choosing, very slowly, whom to tell. His record is the spine of the chapter: what he wrote at the time, against what he remembered later.

eyes.name: Emma Darwin (née Wedgwood)
eyes.role: Darwin's first cousin, aged 30 at their engagement in November 1838; his wife from 29 January 1839
eyes.side: Wedgwood family of Maer; devout Unitarian-leaning Anglican
eyes.where: Maer Hall, Staffordshire, then London and Down
eyes.vantage_label: the first person told of his doubts
eyes.authenticity: Her letters of November 1838 and c. February 1839 survive in the Darwin Archive, Cambridge, and are edited by the Darwin Correspondence Project; the second is dated only approximately by the editors. Darwin kept the February letter all his life.
eyes.bio: Darwin told her of his religious doubts before they married, and her two letters are the earliest surviving response anyone made to his private thinking. She did not argue science; she argued about truth, proof and what might be lost between them. In 1844 she was also the person he trusted to publish the theory if he died.

sources.title: Emma Darwin to Darwin, c. February 1839 (DCP)

eyes.name: Joseph Dalton Hooker
eyes.role: Botanist, aged 26 in January 1844, recently back from the Antarctic voyage of the Erebus and Terror and working on its plants
eyes.vantage_label: the trusted reader, told in a letter
eyes.authenticity: Letters edited by the Darwin Correspondence Project from the originals at Cambridge and Kew; dates on Hooker's side are mostly his own.
eyes.bio: A new correspondent whom Darwin chose as his first scientific confidant. His reply of 29 January 1844 is the first recorded scientific response to Darwin's heresy: open, unconvinced, curious. Over the next year the two men tested each other's views and read Vestiges side by side.

eyes.name: Leonard Jenyns (later Blomefield)
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. Clergyman-naturalist, vicar of Swaffham Bulbeck, Cambridgeshire; aged 44 in 1844. His reply to Darwin's letter of October 1844 is not known to survive; his reaction is known only from Darwin's answer of 25 November 1844.
eyes.authenticity: Darwin's letters to him of 12 October and 25 November 1844 survive; the DCP editors note there is no record that Jenyns ever read the essay.
eyes.bio: Jenyns had described the Beagle fishes and was a careful, conservative naturalist and priest. Darwin's October 1844 letter told him plainly that species are mutable. Darwin's follow-up shows that Jenyns took his words as a firmer claim than Darwin meant.

eyes.name: Sir Charles Lyell
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found for 1837–44 of his knowing Darwin's theory. Geologist, author of the Principles of Geology, Darwin's mentor in London; aged 40 in 1837. His first known written notes on Darwin's theory date from 16 April 1856.
eyes.side: London scientific establishment; opponent of transmutation in the Principles
eyes.form: recorded in Darwin's letters (his own scientific journals on species begin in 1855)
eyes.authenticity: Darwin's letter to him of [14] September 1838 and the 5 July 1844 instructions to Emma are the period records; Lyell's own notes of 16 April 1856 belong to the later story.
eyes.bio: Lyell knew Darwin was filling notebooks on the species question from 1838, and in 1844 Darwin named him first choice to edit the essay. Yet in this period no letter is known in which Darwin set out his conclusion to him. The man whose geology made the theory thinkable was among the last of the inner circle to hear it in full.

sources.title: DCP: Evolution commentary (letter to Lyell, [14] Sept 1838)

eyes.name: John Stevens Henslow
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found of his response to Darwin's species views in this period. Professor of botany at Cambridge and, from 1837, rector of Hitcham, Suffolk; Darwin's old teacher, who had put him forward for the Beagle.
eyes.authenticity: Known here only through Darwin's 5 July 1844 letter to Emma and the DCP editors' notes.
eyes.bio: The man who had sent Darwin round the world appears in the 1844 instructions as 'quite best in many respects' as editor, but Darwin added question marks to his name. The doubt seems to be about whether a clergyman and busy parish rector would or could take on a book of this kind. Henslow's own view of the theory before 1859 is not on record here.

eyes.name: Robert Waring Darwin
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. Physician at Shrewsbury, Darwin's father, aged 72 in 1838. His advice on religious doubt in marriage is known only from his son's Autobiography.
eyes.authenticity: The advice appears in the full text of the Autobiography (Barlow 1958, p. 95), cut from the 1887 printing; the DCP editors cite it in a note to Emma's letter of November 1838.
eyes.bio: A shrewd doctor who kept his own scepticism out of family view. By his son's account he advised Darwin to conceal his doubts from his future wife. Darwin did the opposite, and Emma's letters are the result.

sources.title: Emma Wedgwood to Darwin, [21–2 Nov 1838], note 2 (DCP)

eyes.name: Robert Chambers
eyes.role: Edinburgh publisher and writer, co-owner of W. & R. Chambers, aged 42 in 1844; the secret author of Vestiges
eyes.side: Scottish popular publishing; phrenology and reform circles
eyes.vantage_label: the other man with a secret
eyes.form: anonymous book (Vestiges, October 1844) and its anonymous sequel (Explanations, 1845)
eyes.authenticity: Vestiges was published anonymously by John Churchill, London, in October 1844; Chambers's authorship was acknowledged only in the 12th edition of 1884, after his death. His letters to Alexander Ireland survive and are the basis of J. A. Secord's Victorian Sensation (2000); they were not consulted for this chapter.
eyes.bio: While Darwin hid a theory, Chambers hid a name. He wrote a sweeping, readable case for the development of all life under natural law and published it with elaborate precautions against detection. Its noisy reception showed Darwin exactly what his own ideas would face.

sources.title: Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation (1844), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Alexander Ireland
eyes.role: Manchester businessman and journalist, Chambers's friend, aged 34 in 1844; the go-between who carried manuscript, proofs and letters
eyes.form: introduction to the 12th edition of Vestiges (1884), a later firsthand account
eyes.authenticity: His account of the secrecy was printed forty years after the event, when he brought out the 1884 edition under Chambers's name.
eyes.bio: Ireland's address stood between Chambers and the London trade, so that no letter, proof or payment could be traced to Edinburgh. In 1884 he ended the anonymity and told how it had been kept. His late telling is a ledger point of its own.

sources.title: Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation (overview, Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Adam Sedgwick
eyes.role: Woodwardian Professor of Geology at Cambridge and canon of Norwich, aged 60 in 1845; Darwin's former geology teacher
eyes.side: Cambridge; Church of England; natural theology
eyes.form: dated letters (printed 1890) and an anonymous-by-convention but openly attributed review (1845)
eyes.authenticity: Letter to Lyell of 9 April 1845 printed in Clark and Hughes, Life and Letters of the Reverend Adam Sedgwick (1890), vol. 2. Review in the Edinburgh Review, vol. 82 (July 1845), pp. 1–85.
eyes.bio: Sedgwick had taken Darwin on a geological tour of North Wales in 1831. In 1845 he led the attack on Vestiges with an 85-page review, arguing that if development were true, religion and morality fell with it. Darwin read the review as a preview of what would be said of him.

sources.title: Sedgwick quotations on Vestiges (Today in Science, citing Clark & Hughes 1890)

eyes.name: Alfred Russel Wallace
eyes.role: Former land surveyor and schoolteacher, aged 22 in 1845, running his late brother's business in Neath and collecting beetles
eyes.vantage_label: a young reader far from the inner circle
eyes.authenticity: Letters to H. W. Bates of 9 November and 28 December 1845 survive at the Natural History Museum, London (WP1/3/17) and are edited by the Wallace Correspondence Project.
eyes.bio: Wallace knew nothing of Darwin's essay. He read Vestiges in Wales and, unlike the professors, treated it as a hypothesis worth testing in the field. Thirteen years later his own theory would force Darwin's secret into the open.

eyes.name: Alfred Tennyson
eyes.role: Poet, aged 35 in 1844, at work on the elegies that became In Memoriam (1850)
eyes.where: England, writing to his London publisher Edward Moxon
eyes.vantage_label: a poet who had been thinking the same thoughts
eyes.form: dated letter (printed in Hallam Tennyson's Memoir, 1897)
eyes.authenticity: The November 1844 letter to Moxon is known from its printing in the Memoir by his son (1897) and later biographies; the original was not seen for this chapter.
eyes.bio: Tennyson had been brooding on geology, extinction and a nature indifferent to species for a decade. When Vestiges was advertised he asked for it at once, saying it seemed to touch his own long speculations. He stands for the wider culture that was already half-ready for the idea Darwin was hiding.

sources.title: Andrew Lang, Alfred Tennyson (text quoting the Moxon letter)

entries.headline: Opening a notebook on the transmutation of species
entries.digest: Darwin began a pocket notebook, B, on the 'transmutation of species'. In his Journal he traced the impulse to the South American fossils and, above all, the Galapagos species, which had struck him since about March. On page 36 he drew a small branching tree headed 'I think', a picture of common descent meant for no one else.
entries.quote: In July opened first note book on "Transmutation of Species"
entries.source_note: Darwin's 'Journal', 1837 (de Beer 1959, Darwin Online); Notebook B, CUL DAR 121 p. 36; DCP 'I think' page. The Journal entry was written in retrospectively, as the Journal was begun in 1838.

entries.headline: 'Work finished If not marry': the first reckoning
entries.digest: On a scrap of paper Darwin set out two futures. Unmarried, he would travel and do geology and zoology; married, he would need a post, perhaps a Cambridge professorship, and live modestly. Either way the science would go on.
entries.quote: My destiny will be Camb. Prof. or poor man
entries.source_note: Memorandum CUL DAR 210.8.1 (Darwin Online, ed. van Wyhe), dated by the editors to after 7 April 1838; exact date unknown.

entries.headline: Unwell, and working at 'species'
entries.digest: A bare pocket-journal line records him unwell while working at geology and at 'species'. The Journal for these months keeps noting time lost to illness. The note is the private bookkeeping of a man whose real project had no public name.
entries.quote: May 1st Unwell, working at Geolog: as named & "species".
entries.source_note: Darwin's 'Journal', 1838 (de Beer 1959, Darwin Online).

entries.headline: 'This is the question': marry or not marry
entries.digest: In a second note, laid out in two columns, he weighed children, a companion and a home against freedom, clubs, books and the 'terrible loss of time'. He pictured a bachelor life spent like a worker bee and found it intolerable. The note ends in a mock proof.
entries.quote: Marry — Marry — Marry  Q.E.D.
entries.source_note: Memorandum CUL DAR 210.8.2, 'This is the Question' (Darwin Online). The month is the usual editorial dating, not stated on the paper.

entries.headline: Two notebooks opened side by side: species and mind
entries.digest: On the same day Darwin began Notebook D on transmutation and Notebook M on 'metaphysics', morals and expression. From now on the question of how species change ran alongside the question of whether thought and belief were products of the brain. He kept both for himself.
entries.source_note: Notebook D, p. 1 heading 'July 15th 1838 Finished October 2d' (Darwin Online); Notebook M first entry 15 July 1838 per Barrett 1974 (Darwin Online).

entries.headline: A note to himself on how to disguise materialism
entries.digest: Among the M notebook's entries he wrote himself a tactic: to avoid saying how far he believed in materialism, he could speak only of emotions and instincts as hereditary. It is a rare moment where the notebook plans its own concealment. The idea that mind was inherited from animals was the most dangerous part of the whole scheme.
entries.quote: To avoid stating how far, I believe, in Materialism
entries.source_note: Notebook M (CUL DAR 125), undated entry between those of 22 July and 7 August 1838, in Barrett, Metaphysics, Materialism and the Evolution of Mind (1974), Darwin Online.

entries.headline: 'Origin of man now proved'
entries.digest: Darwin wrote that the origin of man was now proved and that metaphysics must flourish. Whoever understood the baboon, he added, would do more for philosophy than Locke. The confident tone belongs to a private page; nothing like it was said aloud for decades.
entries.quote: He who understand baboon would do more toward metaphysics than Locke
entries.source_note: Notebook M, entry of 16 August 1838 (Barrett 1974 printing, Darwin Online).

entries.headline: Telling Lyell only that the notebooks are filling
entries.digest: To Lyell, Darwin wrote that he had been filling notebook after notebook on the question of species. Facts, he said, were beginning to group themselves under sub-laws. He told his mentor that he was working on the problem, not what he had concluded.
entries.quote: which begin to group themselves clearly under sub-laws
entries.source_note: Darwin to Lyell, [14] September [1838] (DCP-LETT-428), as quoted in the DCP Evolution commentary; date editorial.

entries.headline: Malthus, and a hundred thousand wedges
entries.digest: Reading Malthus on population, Darwin wrote that no one before had clearly seen the great check on numbers. He imagined every species thinned year by year by hawks and cold, and nature as a force driving fitted forms into its gaps. Within a single notebook page the mechanism of the theory appears.
entries.quote: One may say there is a force like a hundred thousand wedges trying force every kind of adapted structure into the gaps in the oeconomy of nature, or rather forming gaps by thrusting out weaker ones.
entries.source_note: Notebook D (CUL DAR 123), pp. 134e–135e, entry marked '28th' (Darwin Online transcription; struck-out words omitted).

entries.headline: Notebook E: 'my theory' meets its objections
entries.digest: In the new notebook E, opened as D closed, Darwin began answering critics who did not yet exist. The first was that little change had been seen in historical times. He now called it, privately, 'my theory'.
entries.quote: It cannot be objected to my theory, that the amount of change within historical times has been small
entries.source_note: Notebook E (CUL DAR 124), p. 4, 'October 4th' (Darwin Online). Notebook N, on mind, was begun 2 October 1838 (Barrett 1974).

entries.headline: A father's advice: keep your doubts to yourself
entries.digest: Before the marriage Robert Darwin advised his son to hide his religious doubts carefully from his wife, because such doubts could cause great misery in a marriage. The only record is his son's memory of it nearly forty years later. Darwin did not follow it.
entries.form: reported speech in a later autobiography
entries.source_note: Darwin's Autobiography (written 1876), full text in Barlow ed. 1958, p. 95, as cited in DCP note 2 to Emma's letter of [21–2 Nov 1838]. Month inferred.

entries.headline: 'The day of days': Emma accepts
entries.digest: Two days after reaching Maer, Darwin proposed to his cousin Emma Wedgwood and was accepted. His Journal gives the day three words and an exclamation mark. Before or around the engagement he told her of his doubts about Christianity.
entries.quote: The day of days!
entries.source_note: Darwin's 'Journal', 1838 (de Beer 1959), with editor's note identifying the day of acceptance.

entries.headline: Emma: thank you for your openness
entries.digest: Writing from Maer after he left, Emma said that while he was with her sad thoughts stayed away, but now a fear had crept in that they differed on the most important subject. Her reason told her that honest doubts could not be a sin, yet she felt they would leave a painful gap between them. She thanked him for telling her and said she would dread his hiding his opinions to spare her.
entries.quote: I should dread the feeling that you were concealing your opinions from the fear of giving me pain.
entries.source_note: Emma Wedgwood to Darwin, [21–2 November 1838] (DCP-LETT-441); date from postmark 23 NO 1838.

entries.headline: Married at Maer
entries.digest: Darwin married Emma at Maer and the couple went straight back to London. His Journal notes his age, thirty. The species notebooks continued in the new house in Upper Gower Street.
entries.quote: Jany 29th Married at Maer 30 years old & returned to London.
entries.source_note: Darwin's 'Journal', 1839 (de Beer 1959).

entries.headline: Emma on proof, revelation and fear
entries.digest: Shortly after the wedding Emma wrote him a letter rather than speak. She granted that he was acting conscientiously and sincerely seeking truth, but warned that the scientific habit of believing nothing until proved could be carried into matters beyond proof. Giving up revelation, she argued, carried a danger that keeping it did not. Everything that concerned him concerned her.
entries.quote: there is a danger in giving up revelation which does not exist on the other side
entries.source_note: Emma Darwin to Darwin, c. February 1839 (DCP-LETT-471), date editorial; Darwin's pencil note in the Autobiography manuscript recalls 'her beautiful letter'.

entries.headline: The last transmutation notebook closed
entries.digest: Darwin wrote on the cover of Notebook E that it was finished. Two years of notebooks on species now sat in his study, read by no one. He did not yet write a sketch, by his own later account to guard against prejudice.
entries.quote: Finished July 10th 1839
entries.source_note: Notebook E inside front cover (Darwin Online).

entries.headline: A thirty-five page pencil sketch
entries.digest: Away from London, staying with both families, Darwin wrote his theory out for the first time as a connected argument, in pencil. It opens with variation under domestication and has a section headed 'Natural Selection', the first use of the phrase in his papers. The Journal records illness eating the rest of the year.
entries.quote: During my stay at Maer & Shrewsbury, (5 years after commencement) wrote pencil sketch of my Species theory.
entries.source_note: Darwin's 'Journal', 1842; Pencil sketch CUL DAR 6.16–50 (Darwin Online); 'Mid-summer of 1842' in the 1844 Journal entry; 'June 1842' in the Autobiography. Detailed treatment in v4:darwin-wallace.

entries.headline: Following Emma to Down
entries.digest: Emma moved into Down House on 14 September and Darwin followed three days later. The village sixteen miles from London gave him privacy, a garden and room for experiments. It would be his home for the rest of his life.
entries.quote: Emma came to Down September 14th & I followed on 17th. Sept.
entries.source_note: Darwin's 'Journal', 1842 (de Beer 1959).

entries.headline: 'Like confessing a murder'
entries.digest: Answering a letter from the young botanist Hooker, Darwin explained that the Galapagos and the fossils had set him collecting every fact bearing on what species are. Then he confessed his conclusion, in brackets. He disowned Lamarck's mechanisms but admitted his conclusions were not far from Lamarck's, and claimed, with a joke at his own presumption, to have found the simple way species become adapted.
entries.quote: At last gleams of light have come, & I am almost convinced (quite contrary to opinion I started with) that species are not (it is like confessing a murder) immutable.
entries.source_note: Darwin to J. D. Hooker, 'Thursday', editorially dated [11 January 1844] (DCP-LETT-729, DCP transcription). One DCP feature page gives 5 January.

entries.headline: Hooker: delighted to hear how
entries.digest: Hooker did not recoil. He thought there might have been creations in different places and a gradual change of species, and said no current opinion satisfied him. He asked Darwin to tell him how the change might happen.
entries.quote: There may in my opinion have been a series of productions on different spots, & also a gradual change of species. I shall be delighted to hear how you think that this change may have taken place, as no presently conceived opinions satisfy me on the subject.
entries.source_note: Hooker to Darwin, 29 January 1844, Kew (DCP-LETT-734).

entries.headline: A letter to be opened if he dies
entries.digest: Having finished the expanded essay, Darwin wrote to Emma a request to be treated as part of his will. She was to spend £400 to have it edited and published, give the editor his annotated books, and promote it herself or through her brother Hensleigh. He ranked possible editors: Lyell best, Henslow perhaps, Hooker added in the margin.
entries.quote: I have just finished my sketch of my species theory. If, as I believe that my theory is true & if it be accepted even by one competent judge, it will be a considerable step in science.
entries.source_note: Darwin to Emma Darwin, 5 July 1844 (DCP-LETT-761, Epsilon transcription). Printed in Life and Letters (1887).

entries.headline: Entrusted with the essay
entries.digest: The letter made Emma the executor of the theory she feared for. No reply from her is known; the instruction was for a future that did not come. Ten years later Darwin added on the cover that Hooker was by far the best man to edit it.
entries.source_note: DCP-LETT-761 and its cover endorsement 'Aug. 1854' (Epsilon transcription). No reply survives.

entries.headline: Named first choice as editor
entries.digest: In the instructions to Emma, Darwin wrote that Lyell would be the best editor if he would undertake it, and that he would find the work pleasant and learn facts new to him. No sign survives that Lyell was told of the choice at the time.
entries.quote: Mr. Lyell would be the best if he would undertake it
entries.source_note: Darwin to Emma Darwin, 5 July 1844 (DCP-LETT-761).

entries.headline: Named, with question marks
entries.digest: Darwin rated his old teacher the next best editor, and in many respects the best, then added two question marks after the name. Henslow is not known to have seen the essay. The doubt on the page is Darwin's, not his.
entries.quote: The next best (& quite best in many respects) would be Professor Henslow??
entries.source_note: DCP-LETT-761; DCP editors note that Darwin queried Henslow's name.

entries.headline: The essay goes to the copyist
entries.digest: The same day his Journal records sending the written sketch, about 230 pages, seven years after he began, to a Mr Fletcher to be copied. The fair copy made it a document that could survive him. Only a handful of people would ever see it before 1858.
entries.quote: Sent a written Sketch of Species theory (seven years after commencement) in about 230 pages
entries.source_note: Darwin's 'Journal', 1844 (de Beer 1959). The Autobiography also says 230 pages.

entries.headline: Vestiges appears without a name
entries.digest: An anonymous book, Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, set out a universe developing by law from nebula to man. Its central hypothesis was that the simplest forms gave birth, step by step, to higher ones. Reviews began in mid-November and it became a sensation.
entries.quote: the simplest and most primitive type, under a law to which that of like-production is subordinate, gave birth to the type next above it
entries.source_note: Vestiges (London: John Churchill, 1844), chapter 'Hypothesis of the Development of the Vegetable and Animal Kingdoms' (Project Gutenberg); publication month from Secord and Wikipedia.

entries.headline: Proofs routed through Manchester
entries.digest: Chambers wrote the book at St Andrews and his wife copied each section so his hand would not be recognised. Ireland delivered the manuscript to London, and the printer's proofs came back to him to be forwarded. Only four people knew the author's name.
entries.source_note: Ireland's introduction to the 12th edition (1884), as summarised in the Wikipedia article on Vestiges (drawing on Secord); not read directly.

entries.headline: Telling Jenyns: species are mutable
entries.digest: Asking his clergyman friend for facts on what checks the increase of a species, Darwin explained that his reading had a purpose. He stated his conclusion outright and admitted it laid him open to reproach. He would not publish for several years; for now, he said, he was on the geology of South America.
entries.quote: The general conclusion at which I have slowly been driven from a directly opposite conviction is that species are mutable & that allied species are co-descendants of common stocks. I know how much I open myself, to reproach, for such a conclusion, but I have at least honestly & deliberately come to it.
entries.source_note: Darwin to Leonard Jenyns, 12 October [1844] (DCP-LETT-782, Epsilon transcription); year editorial.

entries.headline: Jenyns replies (letter lost)
entries.digest: Jenyns answered Darwin's confession; the letter is not known to survive. From Darwin's response it seems Jenyns understood him to claim his conclusions were inevitable. There is no record that he ever read the essay itself.
entries.source_note: Inferred from Darwin to Jenyns, 25 [November 1844] (DCP-LETT-793) and its editorial note.

entries.headline: Tennyson asks for the advertised book
entries.digest: Seeing Vestiges advertised in the Examiner, Tennyson asked his publisher Moxon to get it for him. He wrote that it seemed to contain speculations he had long been familiar with, ones he had already put into poems. He was then writing the elegies of In Memoriam.
entries.quote: I want you to get me a book which I see advertised in the Examiner
entries.source_note: Tennyson to Edward Moxon, November 1844, as printed in Hallam Tennyson's Memoir (1897) and quoted in Lang's Alfred Tennyson; day not known.

entries.headline: To Hooker: two sides to the question
entries.digest: Darwin pressed Hooker on the immutability of species, arguing that the question had two sides. The letters now traded facts on island floras and distribution. The confession of January had become a working argument between two naturalists.
entries.quote: there are two sides to the question of the immutability of species
entries.source_note: Darwin to Hooker, [10–11 November 1844] (DCP-LETT-789), as quoted in the DCP Evolution commentary; date editorial.

entries.headline: 'Thought a complete fool, & a most deliberate one'
entries.digest: Darwin wrote again to Jenyns to correct an impression: he had not meant that his conclusions were inevitable. In his wildest daydream he hoped only to show the question had two sides, admitting immense difficulties, though fewer than on the common view. He called himself a bold man to risk being thought a fool.
entries.quote: I am a bold man to lay myself open to being thought a complete fool, & a most deliberate one.
entries.source_note: Darwin to Jenyns, 25 [November 1844] (DCP-LETT-793, Epsilon transcription).

entries.headline: Hooker on Vestiges: a nine days' wonder
entries.digest: Hooker told Darwin he had been delighted by the range of facts in Vestiges but did not agree with its conclusions at all. He asked what really separated it from Lamarck, whom its author mocked. He guessed it would not last.
entries.quote: somehow the books looks more like a 9 days wonder than a lasting work
entries.source_note: Hooker to Darwin, 30 December 1844 (DCP-LETT-804, Epsilon transcription).

entries.headline: Darwin on Vestiges: bad geology, worse zoology
entries.digest: Darwin replied that he had read the book too and been less amused than Hooker. He admired the writing and arrangement but judged its science poor. The book that said in public what he believed in private was, to him, an argument done badly.
entries.quote: I have, also, read the Vestiges, but have been somewhat less amused at it, than you appear to have been: the writing & arrangement are certainly admirable, but his geology strikes me as bad, & his zoology far worse.
entries.source_note: Darwin to Hooker, [7 January 1845] (DCP-LETT-814, Epsilon transcription); date editorial.

entries.headline: Sedgwick to Lyell: 'the foul book'
entries.digest: Sedgwick wrote to Lyell in fury about Vestiges, saying it reasoned from principles opposed to all sober inductive truth. If it were true, he argued, the work of science was vain and religion, law and morals would fall. The same letter guessed at who could have written it.
entries.quote: If the Vestiges be true, the labours of sober induction are in vain; religion is a lie;
entries.source_note: Sedgwick to Lyell, 9 April 1845, in Clark and Hughes, Life and Letters of the Reverend Adam Sedgwick (1890), vol. 2, p. 84, as quoted by Today in Science; the 'foul book' phrase per Wikipedia.

entries.headline: Suspected of the authorship
entries.digest: In a family letter to his cousin Fox, Darwin called Vestiges strange and unphilosophical but capitally written. It had made more talk than any recent book and some attributed it to him. He felt both flattered and unflattered.
entries.quote: it has made more talk than any work of late, & has been by some attributed to me.
entries.source_note: Darwin to W. D. Fox, [24 April 1845] (DCP-LETT-859); date editorial.

entries.headline: Eighty-five pages in the Edinburgh Review
entries.digest: Sedgwick's review of Vestiges filled pp. 1–85 of the Edinburgh Review. Formally anonymous, it was known to be his. It attacked the book's science and its morals, and was read in learned circles as the verdict of Cambridge.
entries.source_note: Edinburgh Review vol. 82 (1845), pp. 1–85 (DCP 'Darwin's letters 1844–1846'); July issue per Wikipedia.

entries.headline: More kicks than half-pennies
entries.digest: Writing to Hooker, Darwin said that whatever the abuse, he would attempt his species work if he lived. The public storm over Vestiges had not stopped him; it had told him the price. He was by now embarking on years of other work first.
entries.quote: though I shall get more kicks than half-pennies, I will, life serving, attempt my work
entries.source_note: Darwin to Hooker, [10 September 1845] (DCP-LETT-915), as quoted in the DCP Evolution commentary.

entries.headline: Reading Sedgwick 'with fear & trembling'
entries.digest: To Lyell, Darwin judged Sedgwick's review a grand argument against the mutability of species, though some passages smacked more of the pulpit than the professor's chair. He confessed he had read it fearfully, and was relieved that he had not overlooked any of its arguments. He did not say why the arguments concerned him so closely.
entries.quote: I read it with fear & trembling, but was well pleased to find, that I had not overlooked any of the arguments
entries.source_note: Darwin to Lyell, 8 October [1845], Shrewsbury (DCP-LETT-919, Epsilon transcription).

entries.headline: Wallace asks Bates: have you read Vestiges?
entries.digest: In a letter mostly about beetles, Wallace asked his friend Bates whether he had read Vestiges or whether it was out of his line. The book had reached a young collector in South Wales within a year. It was the start of an argument by post.
entries.quote: Have you read "Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation"?
entries.source_note: Wallace to H. W. Bates, 9 November 1845 (WCP345).

entries.headline: An anonymous reply to the critics
entries.digest: Chambers answered the reviewers, Sedgwick above all, with Explanations: A Sequel, a 206-page defence credited only to 'the author of that work'. He kept his name hidden while arguing in public. The secret author and the secret theorist were both, in their ways, refusing to be seen.
entries.source_note: Explanations (London: John Churchill, 1845), details as given in the Wikipedia article on Vestiges; month approximate.

entries.headline: Wallace: an ingenious hypothesis to be tested
entries.digest: Wallace told Bates he thought better of Vestiges than Bates did. He did not see it as a rash generalisation but as a hypothesis supported by striking facts that still needed proof. Every observer's facts, he argued, would now count for or against it.
entries.quote: I have rather a more favorable opinion of the "Vestiges" than you appear to have ... I do not consider it as a hasty generalizsation, but rather as an ingenious hypothesis strongly supported by some striking facts and analogies but which remains to be proved by more facts
entries.source_note: Wallace to Bates, 28 December 1845, Neath (WCP346; NHM WP1/3/17); spelling as transcribed.

entries.headline: Remembering Malthus as 'October 1838'
entries.digest: Writing his recollections for his family, Darwin placed the Malthus reading in October 1838 and said the idea struck him at once. He added that he was so anxious to avoid prejudice that he would not write even a brief sketch for some time. The notebook of 28 September tells the same story a little earlier and more untidily.
entries.quote: In October 1838, that is, fifteen months after I had begun my systematic enquiry, I happened to read for amusement 'Malthus on Population,'
entries.source_note: Autobiography (written 1876; printed in Life and Letters, 1887), Monadnock transcription.

entries.headline: Forty years on, the name is printed
entries.digest: Ireland brought out the twelfth edition of Vestiges with Robert Chambers's name on it, thirteen years after Chambers's death. His introduction told how the secret had been kept. The anonymity had outlasted its author.
entries.source_note: Vestiges, 12th edn (1884), as described in the Wikipedia article on Vestiges.

convergences.label: September 1838: notebooks filling, and Malthus
convergences.note: On [14] September Darwin told Lyell only that facts were grouping under sub-laws; a fortnight later, alone with Notebook D, he wrote the wedges passage. The mentor heard about the work, never the breakthrough.

convergences.label: November 1838: engagement and the question of doubt
convergences.note: Darwin's Journal marks 11 November as 'the day of days'; his father, by later report, had urged silence about religion; Emma's letter of 21–22 November thanks him for not keeping it. Three records, three positions on secrecy inside a marriage.

convergences.label: January 1844: the first confession and the first reply
convergences.note: Darwin's letter puts the heresy in brackets, 'like confessing a murder'; Hooker's reply eighteen days later treats it as an open question and asks for the mechanism. The test of a secret is the first listener's response.

convergences.label: 5 July 1844: the essay finished, copied and entrusted
convergences.note: In one day Darwin sent the essay to be copied, wrote Emma her instructions, and ranked his possible editors: Lyell first, Henslow queried, Hooker added in the margin. No record shows that the named men were told.

convergences.label: October 1844: one confession, one anonymous book
convergences.note: On 12 October Darwin told Jenyns species are mutable and that he would not publish for years. That same month Chambers's book, routed through Ireland, put development before the public with no name attached.

convergences.label: November–December 1844: Vestiges is read
convergences.note: Tennyson sent for the book, finding his own speculations in it; Darwin, writing to Jenyns, feared being thought a fool; Hooker called Vestiges a nine days' wonder. The public and private versions of the idea now ran side by side.

convergences.label: Spring 1845: suspicion and fury
convergences.note: On 9 April Sedgwick wrote to Lyell that if Vestiges were true religion was a lie; on 24 April Darwin told Fox, half amused, that some thought he had written it. The teacher's rage was the reception the pupil was rehearsing for.

convergences.label: Autumn 1845: reading the reception
convergences.note: Darwin read Sedgwick's review 'with fear & trembling'; Wallace in Neath called Vestiges an ingenious hypothesis; Chambers answered anonymously in Explanations. The same book was a warning to one reader and an invitation to another.

ties.note: First cousins, married 29 January 1839. Her letters about his doubts and his letter about the essay bracket the chapter.
Father and son. The father's advice to conceal doubts survives only in the son's later memory.
Darwin chose Hooker as his first scientific confidant in January 1844; they then read and debated Vestiges by letter.
Cambridge friends; Jenyns described the Beagle fishes. Darwin told him his conclusion in October 1844.
Henslow was married to Jenyns's sister Harriet; both belonged to the Cambridge clerical natural-history circle.
Henslow taught Darwin botany at Cambridge and put him forward for the Beagle; in 1844 Darwin named him, with question marks, as a possible editor.
Lyell's geology shaped Darwin's thinking and Darwin wrote to him of the species notebooks in 1838, yet did not set out his conclusion to him in these years.
Sedgwick took Darwin on a geological tour of North Wales in 1831; in 1845 Darwin read his former teacher's attack on Vestiges as a test of his own case.
Sedgwick's private outburst against Vestiges in April 1845 was addressed to Lyell, who also received Darwin's comments on the review that October.
Sedgwick's 85-page review was the main target of Chambers's anonymous Explanations of 1845.
Friends; Ireland was the intermediary who kept Chambers's authorship secret for forty years and revealed it in 1884.
Darwin read Vestiges critically and was rumoured to be its author; he became convinced Chambers wrote it after meeting him in 1847.
Reading Vestiges in 1845 inclined Wallace towards transmutation, the road that led to his own theory in 1858.
Tennyson sent for Vestiges in November 1844, finding in it ideas he had been working into his poems.

threads_out.note: The 1844 essay, the trusted readers and the letter to Emma are the background to 1858, when Wallace's paper reached Down and Hooker and Lyell, the men Darwin had partly told, arranged the joint reading at the Linnean Society.

Darwin's ambition to be a travelling naturalist came from reading Humboldt's Personal Narrative; the observations of the Beagle voyage that Humboldt inspired are what the transmutation notebooks set out to explain.
The Malthus whose Essay on Population triggered the wedges passage in 1838 was also the authority behind the population and relief arguments of British officials during the Irish famine of 1845–52.
Darwin's Malthus moment, recorded in the notebook as a working entry and remembered in 1876 as a sudden flash, is a case of an idea's arrival being retold as more instant than the record shows.
